A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TextMesh4D, with readable text, equations, tables, and figures across all 11 pages. Both end with references and contain no appendices. Referenced supplementary documents and videos are absent from the supplied PDFs and cannot be assessed.

before.justification: v1 reports original generated meshes, CLIP evaluations, a 31-participant user study, and ablation results in Section 4 and Tables 1–2.

after.justification: v2 retains original generation results and reports expanded baseline comparisons, human evaluations, GPT-4V selections, and ablations in Section 4 and Tables 1–2.

M1.justification: The NeuS initialization, static Jacobian optimization, dynamic delta Jacobians and rigid transformations, diffusion guidance, and regularizers are retained. JDF names the existing parameterization; LGSR groups the existing flexibility and rigidity losses as global and local terms. Algorithm 1 adds documentation without establishing a changed procedure.

E1.justification: Comparison coverage extends to video- and 3D-conditioned generation, including L4GM, 3-to-4D, and Puppeteer in v2 Table 1; v1 compared text-conditioned generation and text-generated image inputs. TextMesh4D itself remains text-conditioned. The reported union of baseline prompt sets does not establish which object domains or prompts changed.

E2.justification: Table 1 expands from two baselines to nine, adding Dream-in-4D, TC4D, AYG, STAG4D, L4GM, 3-to-4D, and Puppeteer. The retained DG4D is DreamGaussian4D under an abbreviated name. CT4D is discussed only through an unavailable supplementary comparison and is not counted as inspected comparative evidence.

E3.justification: v2 introduces zero-shot GPT-4V preference evaluation. Table 1 replaces human vote percentages with scores on an unexplained scale, while Table 2 changes its stated evaluator from humans to GPT-4V. The second vertex ablation is also described as using intermediate rigging instead of a 1000-fold ARAP weight. These are reported protocol revisions, without establishing reruns.

E4.justification: The flag example and regularizer-removal ablations remain after matching renamed components. However, v1's comparison of light versus heavy ARAP weighting becomes v2's direct-vertex versus intermediate-rigging comparison. This revises the documented ablation question, although the reused imagery and nearly identical numbers do not establish a newly performed experiment.

E5.justification: Neither PDF reports generation run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Both retain 31 human participants. Adding GPT-4V evaluation does not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds seven comparator rows and GPT-4V outcomes and replaces the human-study results. DG4D's reported CLIP score changes from 29.17 to 28.70, while TextMesh4D and 4D-fy retain 32.32 and 31.03. These are not established same-setting performance changes. Table 2 changes TextMesh4D's TA value from 65.0% to 66.0% while relabeling the evaluator; the later TA column totals 101%.

T1.justification: The Jacobian/Poisson formulation, mesh-sequence parameterization, and mathematical content of Equations 1–5 are retained under revised notation and grouping. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive derivation appears.

C1.justification: The central text-to-4D generation, quality, and 24GB memory claims remain. v2 additionally claims that JDF frees deformation from topological constraints and presents the regularizer as enforcing local and global semantic coherence, extending v1's emphasis on smooth optimization and balancing flexibility with rigidity.

C2.justification: v2 interprets vertex failures through topology-induced inflexibility and regularizer effects through local noise suppression and global identity preservation. It adds a limitation concerning highly exaggerated motions such as explosions. The earlier limitations involving unsuccessful static initialization and camera-constrained global transformations remain.

D1.justification: Algorithm 1 and Section 4.1 newly disclose Adam, learning rate 0.01, and four regularizer weights. v2 identifies hardware inconsistently as RTX 6000 in the text and A5000 in Table 1. v1's explicit Kling input-generation name and 20-prompt count disappear. Code release remains promised rather than documented as available.

R1.justification: The related-work review is largely retained. v2 adds citations to CT4D, L4GM, STAG4D, Puppeteer, Bringing Objects to Life, and Adam, and removes the standalone original 3D Gaussian Splatting citation. Evaluation positioning broadens to include data-driven and differently conditioned approaches.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution framing, and ablation discussion are extensively rewritten around JDF and LGSR. Method subsections are renamed and reorganized, and experiments gain separate implementation, setup, qualitative, quantitative, and ablation subsections. The title, author list, and affiliations also change.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the overview, consolidates selected teaser and gallery examples into Figure 3, and splits v1's comparison grid into Figures 4–6 with geometry views, close-ups, and motion overlays. Table 1 expands substantially, Algorithm 1 is added, and the ablation display is relocated and relabeled. Much of the imagery is retained rather than newly generated evidence.

improvement.justification: v2 broadens comparisons, adds implementation information, and improves organization. However, Table 2 reattributes almost identical human-study percentages to GPT-4V while redefining a vertex ablation, without explaining the provenance changes; its TA column now totals 101%. Table 1 also replaces explicit vote percentages with an unexplained human-score scale. These issues affect central empirical support, preventing a reliable net quality judgment despite the gains in breadth and presentation.
